processing: Partially oxidised by withering and tossing, then fixed, rolled and dried, as with other Dancong.
harvest_season: Usually spring, as with most Fenghuang Dancong.
appearance_dry: Tightly rolled, stout straight strips like iron nails, pale yellow-brown and glossy.
appearance_liquor: Orange-yellow, as is typical of the Zhi Lan aroma type.
appearance_wet: Long, narrow leaves that show the bamboo-like shape behind the name.
taste_profile: A natural Zhi Lan orchid aroma that is high, sharp and lasting.

brewing.notes: Quick pours keep the sharp orchid top note clean.

vintage_note: As is usual for Dancong, it is sold by harvest year and season, mostly fresh spring tea or tea rested a year or two after roasting. Sellers may list it as Zhu Ye or by its other name, Zhi Lan Wang, which is worth checking.
description:
Zhu Ye means bamboo leaf, a plain description of this Fenghuang strain's long, narrow foliage. Its other name, Zhi Lan Wang, king of Zhi Lan, is a claim about its orchid aroma.

It goes through the usual Dancong steps of withering, tossing, fixing, rolling and drying. The finished strips are distinctive: tight, straight and thick like iron nails, in a pale yellow-brown.

The aroma is what people come for, high and sharp and slow to fade. Use plenty of leaf and short steeps, and let the sweetness build across the session.

The word king is a nickname, not a grade. Judge it by whether the orchid holds across several steeps.
history: Little is documented about when or by whom the strain was selected. Chinese accounts explain both names, one from the leaf shape and the other from the strong orchid scent, and it is now sold abroad under the name Zhu Ye as well.
